title: Visual Studio Code setup
intro: Visual Studio Code on Windows working in WSL Ubuntu: the extensions that fit this toolchain, how each is configured, and a script that installs and configures them from a profile.
scope: Free extensions first. An extension with a paid tier (GitLens) or a proprietary licence (Claude Code, the WSL extension) says so. Versions are the stable Marketplace builds, never the pre-release ones.

entries.name: Start here: VS Code on Windows, working in WSL
entries.summary: Visual Studio Code is installed on Windows. The WSL extension runs your files, terminal and most extensions inside Ubuntu. A script installs the extensions and merges the settings from a profile.

version.name: Visual Studio Code
version.docs: code.visualstudio.com/docs, pages dated 2026-10-28

notes: The start date was not checked. The licence is the one GitHub shows for the repository; the build Microsoft distributes has its own licence terms, which were not read.

setup/setup.sh was tested against a stand-in for VS Code (install order, skipping, failures, settings merging) and with --dry-run against the real install. A real install has not been run yet: that the extensions land in ~/.vscode-server/extensions through `code --install-extension` rests on reading the `code` launcher script and the docs, not on a run.

`code --install-extension` is not described in the pages read as installing a pre-release. The docs only describe the pre-release choice in the Install button's menu, so the CLI is assumed to install the stable build (unconfirmed).

sections.title: In one minute
items: VS Code is a Windows program. With the WSL extension, a window opened from Ubuntu runs the VS Code Server inside WSL: editing, the terminal, git, the debugger and most extensions all use your Linux tools. Only the window itself is on Windows.

items.alt: VS Code and the WSL extension run on Windows. They connect to the VS Code Server inside the WSL Ubuntu VM, where the extensions, the zsh terminal and the repositories in ~/src live.
items.caption: What runs where.

cards.title: Install on Windows
cards.text: Not inside WSL. Check the Add to PATH option so `code` works from Ubuntu.

cards.title: Extensions in WSL
cards.text: Most extensions run inside WSL. Themes and snippets stay on Windows.

cards.title: Open with code .
cards.text: From a folder in Ubuntu. The first time, VS Code fetches what it needs for WSL.

cards.title: Settings are shared
cards.text: User settings apply in WSL windows too. A Remote settings file holds WSL-only values.

sections.title: What this page installs
items: Each row is an extension, with the stable version analysed, the oldest VS Code it runs on, and where `setup.sh` installs it. The profile ([profile.json](../setup/profile.json)) turns each on or off. Details are in the tabs.

items.caption: Generated from the Marketplace and the profile on 2026-10-29.

sections.title: Install VS Code on Windows
items: Install VS Code on the Windows side, not in WSL. When the installer asks for additional tasks, check **Add to PATH**: that is what makes `code` work from the Ubuntu terminal. If `code` is not found, restart the terminal or you did not add VS Code to the PATH.

items.title: Update VS Code first
items.text: Every extension states the oldest VS Code it runs on, and an install fails below it. At the check date GitHub Pull Requests needed 1.144.0, which was the newest release, and Container Tools needed 1.109. The table above lists all of them.

items: `code --version` shows the installed version. This machine had 1.144.0.

sections.title: Run the script
sections.intro: In Ubuntu, as your normal user. No sudo.
items: [setup.sh](../setup/setup.sh) reads [profile.json](../setup/profile.json). `./setup.sh --dry-run` shows what is installed, what would be, and which settings would change. `./setup.sh` does it. `--list` prints the profile, `--only ruff,terraform` runs just those (it matches the part after the publisher, or a settings group), and `--profile my.json` uses another file.

Order: the WSL extension first, on the Windows side, then every other extension inside WSL. This order matters. The `code` launcher checks for the WSL extension and, with it, sends commands to WSL; without it, to Windows.
Settings are merged into the Windows user `settings.json`, keeping what is there. A backup is made first. A file that contains comments is left alone and the script says what to merge by hand.

items.title: Run it again any time
items.text: An extension that is installed is skipped, and a setting already at its value is left alone. After you change the profile, run it again.

sections.title: Open a project and sign in
items: From a folder in Ubuntu, such as `~/src/atlas`, run `code .`. The first time, VS Code fetches the components it needs to run in WSL. A WSL indicator then appears in the bottom left corner.
Sign in from inside VS Code: Claude Code on its first open, and GitHub from the Pull Requests view. Azure Resources has its own sign-in (unconfirmed: its README was not read).
Run `Developer: Reload Window` once if an extension does not show up after installing.

sections.title: Keeping it current
items: Extensions update themselves unless you turn auto update off (the `extensions.autoUpdate` setting, or the Disable Auto Update command). An extension installed from a VSIX file does not auto update.

items.title: Pre-release builds
items.text: Several of these extensions publish a newer pre-release build next to the stable one: Python, YAML, GitHub Pull Requests, GitLens and Dev Containers did on 2026-10-29. The Extensions view installs a pre-release only when you choose Install Pre-Release Version. The versions on this page are the stable ones.

items: `make vscode-check` (from the repository root) compares the stable versions and minimum VS Code on the Marketplace with this page and prints the differences.

sections.title: If something breaks
items: `WSL: Show Log` in the Command Palette shows the WSL log. VS Code starts no shell startup scripts for its server in WSL, so a PATH change in `~/.zshrc` does not reach the server. The terminal inside VS Code does read it. To change the server's environment, use `~/.vscode-server/server-env-setup`, a Bourne shell script: an invalid one stops the server from starting.

To remove all WSL-side extensions: `rm -rf ~/.vscode-server/extensions`. To remove the whole server: `rm -rf ~/.vscode-server`. Both are re-created the next time a window opens (that second command comes from the SSH section of the troubleshooting page; WSL uses the same folder name).

sections.title: Reference
items: Settings Sync is the alternative to a profile in a repository: it keeps preferences, and with the data categories you pick, other things, in step across devices after you sign in with a Microsoft or GitHub account. This repository keeps a profile instead so it can be read, reviewed and versioned.
A project can recommend extensions to everyone who opens it, in `.vscode/extensions.json`:

items.title: Recommended extensions for one project
Install an extension from a terminal

entries.name: WSL
entries.summary: Opens any folder in WSL as a full VS Code workspace. It is the only extension installed on the Windows side, and it must be there before the others, because it decides where `code` sends commands.
entries.license: Microsoft Software License Terms for the Remote Development extensions

version.name: WSL extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.104.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: With the WSL extension, a VS Code window can run in a WSL distribution: "any VS Code operations you perform in this window will be executed in the WSL environment, everything from editing and file operations, to debugging, using terminals, and more."
WSL 1 has known limits for some kinds of development. The WSL 2 setup from the Workstation guide is assumed.

items.title: How the `code` command picks a side
items.text: The `code` script that VS Code installs on Windows asks whether the WSL extension is installed. If it is, commands run through the extension's own script and go to WSL. If it is not, they run on Windows. This was read in the script itself (`bin/code` in the install folder), not in the docs.

sections.title: Install and open a folder
items: Install the extension on Windows (`setup.sh` does it first). With it installed, a Remote Status bar item appears at the far left and shows whether the window is local or in WSL.

From Ubuntu: go to a folder and run `code .`. The first time VS Code fetches the components for WSL, once. From VS Code: `F1`, then `WSL: Connect to WSL` (or `WSL: Connect to WSL using Distro`), then open a folder. `WSL: Reopen Folder in WSL` and `WSL: Reopen in Windows` switch sides.
From a Windows prompt: `code --remote wsl+<distro name> <path in WSL>`.

items.title: Keep projects in the Linux file system
items.text: Open folders under `~` (for example `~/src`), not under `/mnt/c`. The WSL docs say performance is best when files are in the file system of the tools that use them.

sections.title: Extensions and terminals
items: VS Code runs an extension in one of two places: on the Windows side (the UI side) or in WSL. UI extensions, such as themes and snippets, stay local. Most others run in WSL. Installing from the Extensions view puts each in the right place, and groups them under a Local and a WSL heading. A local extension that needs to run in WSL shows dimmed, with an Install button.
The cloud button next to Local - Installed offers Install Local Extensions in WSL to copy several at once. Any terminal opened in a WSL window runs in WSL.
Remote extensions live in `~/.vscode-server/extensions` inside Ubuntu. `setup.sh` checks that folder to confirm an install.

sections.title: Git line endings
items: If Windows and WSL both use the same repository, Git can report many modified files that differ only in line endings. A `.gitattributes` file at the repository root fixes it for everyone, and is the most reliable way:

items.title: Force LF in the repository

items: The same page says it works with Git 2.10 or later. Credentials: the WSL docs describe using the Windows Git Credential Manager, covered in the [Workstation guide](../../workstation/site/index.html).

sections.title: Settings in WSL
items: VS Code's user settings are reused in WSL windows. For values that should differ in WSL, run `Preferences: Open Remote Settings` once connected, or use the Remote tab in the Settings editor.
The remote settings file's path was not given in the pages read, so `setup.sh` writes only to the user settings file.
`remote.extensionKind` can force an extension to run on a chosen side if the extension supports it. See the Containers tab for the documented example.

sources.label: VS Code docs: Developing in WSL
VS Code docs: Remote development in WSL (tutorial)
VS Code docs: Remote development troubleshooting

notes: The WSL extension is closed source: its licence is Microsoft's, not an open source licence. The repository linked on the Marketplace holds the issue tracker.

entries.name: Claude Code for VS Code
entries.summary: Claude Code in a VS Code panel: review plans and diffs, @-mention files and selections, keep conversation history, open several conversations. Needs a paid Claude plan or a Console account.
entries.license: Proprietary (the Marketplace shows no licence file; unconfirmed)

version.name: Claude Code for VS Code extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.94.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: The extension is a graphical interface for Claude Code, and the docs call it the recommended way to use Claude Code in VS Code. It bundles its own copy of the CLI for the chat panel. Its version number is the Claude Code version it bundles.
To run `claude` in VS Code's integrated terminal you also need the standalone CLI. The [Workstation guide](../../workstation/site/index.html) installs it with the native installer.
It needs VS Code 1.94.0 or later, and a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan or a Claude Console account. No API key is required.

sections.title: Install and sign in
items: Installed by `setup.sh` inside WSL. If it does not appear, restart VS Code or run `Developer: Reload Window`.

Open the panel with the Spark icon in the editor toolbar (shown when a file is open), the Spark icon in the Activity Bar, the Status Bar item **Claude Code**, or the Command Palette. The first time, click Sign in and finish in the browser.
Run `Claude Code: Open Walkthrough` from the Command Palette for a guided tour. `Alt+K` inserts an @-mention of your selection.

rows: A classifier reviews most actions instead of asking you. The built-in starting mode with Claude Code 2.1.283 or later.
Claude asks before file edits and most shell commands, and shows a diff you can accept, reject or redirect.
Claude describes what it will do and waits. VS Code opens the plan as a Markdown document where you can comment. `/plan` switches to it.
items.caption: From the Claude Code docs for the VS Code extension.

sections.title: Configure
items: Nothing has to be set. The extension has its own settings (Extensions > Claude Code), and shares `~/.claude/settings.json` with the CLI for allowed commands, environment variables, hooks and MCP servers. Add `"$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json"` to that file for autocomplete and validation in VS Code.

rows: Launch Claude in terminal mode instead of the graphical panel.
Where it opens: `sidebar` (right) or `panel` (a new tab).
The mode new conversations start in: `default`, `plan`, `acceptEdits` or `bypassPermissions`. VS Code reads it from user settings only.
Save files before Claude reads or writes them.
Activate the workspace's Python environment when running Claude. Needs the Python extension.

items.title: In a WSL window, edit settings on the WSL side
items.text: In a window connected to WSL, `~/.claude/settings.json` is the file inside Ubuntu, not the one on Windows. The docs say this when setting `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` for a proxy certificate: save the certificate and edit the file on that system.

sections.title: Reference
items: Whether the extension's panel shows a custom status line set in `~/.claude/settings.json` was not in the pages read (unconfirmed).
More settings exist (`lockEditorGroups`, `attachOpenFile`, `focusView`, `archiveInactiveSessions` and others). The docs list them all with their minimum Claude Code versions.

sources.label: Claude Code docs: Use Claude Code in VS Code
Marketplace: Claude Code for VS Code

notes: The extension has no licence file on the Marketplace and no source repository link there, so the licence is recorded as proprietary but unconfirmed. Claude Code's own repository is shown by GitHub with no licence identifier.

entries.name: Python
entries.summary: Python language support. It installs Pylance (IntelliSense), the Python Debugger and the Python Environments extension, which finds your uv `.venv` folders and uses uv when it is installed.
entries.license: MIT (the extension); Pylance is a proprietary binary; the debugger is MIT

version.name: Python extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.95.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: This one extension is a pack. On 2026-10-29 its extension pack listed Pylance, the Python Debugger (`ms-python.debugpy`) and Python Environments (`ms-python.vscode-python-envs`), so only `ms-python.python` is listed in the profile.
Python Environments "brings environment and package management into Visual Studio Code's UI" for venv, uv, conda, pyenv, poetry and others. It needs no setup: it finds environments on its own.

cards.title: Finds `.venv`
cards.text: Searches the workspace for `./**/.venv` by default, and picks a workspace virtual environment before a system Python.

cards.title: Uses uv
cards.text: If uv is installed, it is used to create environments and install packages. `python-envs.alwaysUseUv` is on by default.

cards.title: Pylance
cards.text: The language server. It ships only in binary form under a Microsoft licence.

sections.title: Use it with uv
items: Create the project with uv (`uv init`, `uv add`, see the Workstation guide). The `.venv` it makes is discovered automatically. If it is not listed, run `Python: Select Interpreter` from the Command Palette and choose it.

items.title: Use uv for every environment (the default)

items: Set it to `false` to use uv only for environments that were created by uv. `Python: Create Environment` makes a new `.venv` with Quick Create or Custom Create.
If an environment is missing, the cause is usually a location outside the search paths: add it to `python-envs.workspaceSearchPaths` or `python-envs.globalSearchPaths`.

sections.title: Formatting and linting
items: The Python extension does not format or lint on its own here. Ruff does both, and its settings are in the Ruff entry, which `setup.sh` turns on together with this one.
Claude Code activates the workspace's Python environment when it runs, through its `claudeCode.usePythonEnvironment` setting.

sections.title: Reference
items: Stable and pre-release: on 2026-10-29 the stable version was 2026.10.0 and a pre-release 2026.11 was published beside it.
The legacy settings `python.venvPath` and `python.venvFolders` are merged into the new search paths automatically.

notes: The pack contents were read from the Marketplace properties on 2026-10-29 and can change with a release.

entries.name: Ruff
entries.summary: Ruff's linter and formatter inside VS Code. It uses the Ruff in your project's environment, then the one on the PATH, then its own bundled copy.

version.name: Ruff extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.91.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Ruff "does not require any additional extensions", but the README recommends the Python Environments or Python extension: with either, Ruff is found in the active environment. If none is found there, the extension checks the PATH, and then uses its bundled executable.
It runs by itself when you open or edit a Python or notebook file, or a Ruff configuration file (`pyproject.toml`, `ruff.toml`, `.ruff.toml`).

sections.title: Format, fix and organise imports on save
items: This is the README's own block, and the one `setup.sh` merges (the `python_ruff` group):

items.title: Format, fix and organise imports on save

items: `source.fixAll` fixes lint violations; `source.organizeImports` sorts imports; `editor.defaultFormatter` makes Ruff the formatter. The README also shows the notebook and Markdown versions.

sections.title: Reference
items: In an untrusted workspace the extension always uses its bundled Ruff and ignores `ruff.path`, `ruff.interpreter`, `ruff.importStrategy`, `ruff.configuration` and `ruff.format.backend`. With Ruff 0.17.0 or later, formatting always uses Ruff's own formatter there.
All extension settings are documented in the Ruff Language Server docs. `ruff.interpreter` points at a Python executable or environment directory when neither Python extension is present.

entries.name: ESLint
entries.summary: Runs ESLint in the editor. It uses the ESLint installed in the project, so ESLint has to be a dependency (with pnpm: `pnpm add --save-dev eslint`).

version.name: ESLint extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.90.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: The extension integrates ESLint into VS Code. It needs ESLint installed locally in the project or globally. A new project may also need a configuration file: for ESLint 9 and later (or 8.57 with flat config) the README lists `eslint.config.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.ts` and `.mts`.
`npx eslint --init` creates a configuration. With ESLint 10 and later, flat config is the default and the `eslint.useFlatConfig` setting is ignored.

sections.title: Fix on save
items: The README's starter setting runs ESLint's fixes when a file is saved. It is in the `eslint` group of the profile:

items.title: Fix ESLint problems on save

items: To limit validation to some languages in one workspace, the README sets `eslint.validate` there.

notes: The README lists installing ESLint with npm, yarn, pnpm and bun; the pnpm command above is its pnpm line.

entries.name: Prettier - Code formatter
entries.summary: Formats JavaScript and TypeScript with Prettier. It uses the project's own Prettier from `node_modules` when there is one, and its bundled Prettier 3 otherwise. The profile makes it format only where a Prettier config file exists.

version.name: Prettier - Code formatter extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.101.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: "This extension bundles Prettier 3.x by default. If your project has a local installation of Prettier (in node_modules), that version will be used instead". Prettier 2.x projects work too. Plugins work when Prettier is resolved locally or globally. In an untrusted workspace only the built-in Prettier is used.

sections.title: Make it the formatter, but only where the project asks
items: VS Code needs to be told which extension formats a language. The README sets `editor.defaultFormatter`, and one block per language: VS Code does not accept `[javascript][typescript]` together.

items.title: Prettier as the default formatter

items: `setup.sh` (group `prettier`) sets it for JavaScript, JavaScript React, TypeScript and TypeScript React, with format on save, and sets `prettier.requireConfig` to `true`. The default of that setting is `false`; with `true`, a file is formatted only if a Prettier configuration file exists, so a repository without one is not reformatted.

items.title: A local config beats VS Code settings
items.text: If any local Prettier configuration file such as `.prettierrc` is present, the VS Code Prettier settings are not used.

items: JSON, YAML and Markdown are left alone on purpose: formatting them on save would rewrite data files such as the JSON in this repository.

entries.name: Kubernetes
entries.summary: A cluster explorer, manifest editing with IntelliSense, logs, port forwarding, and Helm chart tools. It runs your kubectl and helm, so they must be installed.

version.name: Kubernetes extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.110.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: "The extension for developers building applications to run in Kubernetes clusters and for DevOps staff troubleshooting Kubernetes applications." It works with any Kubernetes: Azure, Minikube, AWS, GCP and more.

cards.title: Cluster explorer
cards.text: Browse workloads, services, pods and nodes. Watch resources and see live updates.

cards.title: Manifests
cards.text: IntelliSense for resources, apply to a cluster, diff against the manifest in Git.

cards.title: Helm
cards.text: Syntax highlighting, autocomplete for Helm and Sprig functions, chart scaffolding, lint, template, dry run.

cards.title: Pods
cards.text: Logs, events, a shell in a pod, and local port forwarding.

sections.title: What it needs
items: It needs `kubectl` at minimum, `helm` for Helm features, and `docker` or `buildah` only to build applications. `az`, `minikube` and `git` are optional. The README recommends installing them on the system PATH: some commands do not work otherwise, and the extension offers to install a missing core tool.
The Workstation guide installs kubectl, helm, kind and kubectx in Ubuntu. Because the extension runs in WSL, it finds them there.
It uses your kubeconfig. To point it elsewhere set `vs-kubernetes.kubeconfig`; several files can be listed in `vs-kubernetes.knownKubeconfigs` and switched between.
It depends on the YAML extension, which is installed with it.

sections.title: Reference
items: Commands include `Kubernetes: Explain` (runs `kubectl explain`), `Kubernetes: Add Existing Cluster` (can install kubectl from an AKS cluster), and `Helm: Create Chart`, `Helm: Lint`, `Helm: Preview Template`, `Helm: Dry Run`, `Helm: Package`.

notes: That the extension finds the Linux kubectl when it runs in WSL follows from where extensions run (WSL docs) and from the README's PATH advice; it was not shown in a test here.

entries.name: YAML
entries.summary: YAML validation, completion, hover and formatting through the Red Hat YAML language server, with built-in Kubernetes support and schemas from SchemaStore.

version.name: YAML extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.91.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Built on the `yaml-language-server`. It checks that a file is valid YAML and, with a schema, validates its structure and offers completion. Schema validation supports JSON Schema draft-04, draft-07, 2019-09 and 2020-12.

By default it uses the SchemaStore catalog to attach schemas to common file patterns (`yaml.schemaStore.enable`, default `true`), and validates Kubernetes custom resources against well-known CRD schemas (`yaml.kubernetesCRDStore.enable`, default `true`). Both download schemas, so they need internet access.
The Kubernetes extension installs this one with it.

sections.title: Attach a schema to a file
items: Three ways: a modeline comment at the top of the file, an inline `$schema` property, or the `yaml.schemas` setting that maps a schema (or the keyword `kubernetes`) to glob patterns. `yaml.kubernetesVersion` picks the Kubernetes version when a pattern is mapped to `kubernetes`.

items.title: Point one file at a schema
Do not map every YAML file to Kubernetes
items.text: `setup.sh` sets no `yaml.schemas`. A glob that matches non-Kubernetes YAML would flag it as errors. Use the modeline, or a narrow glob in the workspace settings.

sections.title: Reference
items: By default the extension sets tabs to spaces and a tab size of 2 for YAML files, so indentation stays valid.
Telemetry: the extension sends anonymous usage data to Red Hat when telemetry is on. `redhat.telemetry.enabled` turns it off, and VS Code's `telemetry.telemetryLevel` is honoured.
Stable and pre-release: on 2026-10-29 the stable version was 2.0.0 and a pre-release 2.1 was published beside it.

entries.name: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
entries.summary: Create, manage, deploy and diagnose Azure Kubernetes Service clusters from VS Code.

version.name: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.125.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: The Marketplace describes it as: "Create, manage, deploy, and diagnose AKS clusters directly from VS Code." Its README is short and points to a documentation site for the introduction, installation and feature list.
It needs VS Code 1.125 or later. It is installed next to the Kubernetes extension, not instead of it.

sections.title: Telemetry
items: The README says the extension sends usage data to Microsoft: which commands you run, which screens you open and what you do in them. It says it collects nothing that identifies your code or your Azure resources, such as cluster or resource names, file paths, image names, form input or the contents of your manifests.
To turn telemetry off, set `telemetry.telemetryLevel` to `off`. That applies to VS Code and every extension.

notes: Only the short README and the Marketplace description were read. The features and the Azure sign-in flow are on the documentation site, which was not read (unconfirmed).

entries.name: HashiCorp Terraform
entries.summary: HashiCorp's Terraform extension: syntax highlighting, completion, validation, formatting with `terraform fmt`, and reference counts. It bundles the Terraform language server. It needs `terraform` on the PATH to format.

version.name: HashiCorp Terraform extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.92.2 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: "The Terraform VS Code extension bundles the Terraform Language Server and is a self-contained install." Features: completion of providers, resources, data sources and attributes; validation; formatting; code lens reference counts. It also covers Terraform Stacks, Search and Policy files.
The README says the WSL extension runs this extension directly in WSL, so you can edit files in WSL or on the mounted Windows file system.

items.title: Formatting fails silently without terraform on the PATH
items.text: The README: "Ensure that the terraform binary is present in the environment PATH variable. If the terraform binary cannot be found, formatting will silently fail." The Workstation guide installs Terraform from HashiCorp's apt repository.

sections.title: Format on save
items: The README recommends these settings for the extension. `setup.sh` merges the `[terraform]` and `[terraform-vars]` blocks (the group `terraform`); the README lists more file types:

entries.name: Container Tools
entries.summary: Container Tools: build, manage and deploy containers from VS Code, with Dockerfile and Compose editing help and a container explorer. It is the successor of the Docker extension.

version.name: Container Tools extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.109.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: The extension "makes it easy to build, manage, and deploy containerized applications from Visual Studio Code" and gives one-click debugging of Node.js, Python and .NET inside a container. It needs VS Code 1.109 (January 2026) or later.
The old Docker extension (`ms-azuretools.vscode-docker`) is now a thin extension pack that installs Container Tools, so existing users move forward. This guide installs Container Tools directly.

cards.title: Dockerfile and Compose
cards.text: Completions and syntax help for `Dockerfile` and `compose.yaml`, and errors in the Problems panel.

cards.title: Container Explorer
cards.text: Containers, images, volumes, networks and registries, with a right-click menu.

cards.title: Scaffolding
cards.text: `Containers: Add Docker Files to Workspace` writes a Dockerfile and `.dockerignore` for C#, Node.js, Python, Ruby, Go or Java.

sections.title: What it needs in Ubuntu
items: Docker must be installed and on the PATH. The Workstation guide installs Docker Engine in Ubuntu. On Linux the README advises enabling rootless Docker, or enabling the Docker CLI for the non-root user. The Workstation script adds your user to the `docker` group, which is how Docker's post-install steps let a non-root user run the CLI.
Because the extension runs in WSL, it should use that Docker. That was not tested here (unconfirmed).
If you use Docker Desktop on Windows instead of Docker Engine in Ubuntu, the WSL docs show how to make this extension run on the Windows side:

entries.name: GitHub Pull Requests
entries.summary: Review and manage GitHub pull requests and issues in VS Code: browse, review with in-editor comments, check out, and start working on an issue.

version.name: GitHub Pull Requests extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.144.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Features from the README: sign in and connect VS Code to GitHub and GitHub Enterprise, list and browse PRs, review them with in-editor comments, check them out to validate, terminal integration so the UI and CLIs co-exist, issues, hover cards and completion for users and issues, a "Start working on issue" action that creates a branch, and code actions that create issues from todo comments.
Needs VS Code 1.144.0 or later (the newest release on 2026-10-29). It installs the built-in GitHub Authentication extension as a dependency.

sections.title: Get started
items: Open a GitHub repository. A new view appears in the Activity Bar with pull requests and issues. Use its button to sign in to GitHub.
By default the extension looks for pull requests on the `origin` and `upstream` remotes. If you use other remotes, list them in `githubPullRequests.remotes`.
This sign-in is separate from the GitHub CLI (`gh auth login`) in the Workstation guide. Neither one signs the other in.

sections.title: Reference
items: GitHub Enterprise instances are configured with the built-in `github-enterprise.uris` setting (VS Code 1.141 or later).
Stable and pre-release: on 2026-10-29 the stable version was 0.174.0 and a pre-release 0.175 was published beside it.

entries.name: GitHub Actions
entries.summary: Manage GitHub Actions workflows and runs from the editor, and get validation and completion while writing workflow files.

version.name: GitHub Actions extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.72.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Manage workflows and runs without leaving the editor, follow builds and deployments, investigate failures and read logs. For authoring: syntax highlighting for workflows and expressions, documentation for the workflow schema, validation and completion for the YAML schema and expressions, and for the inputs and outputs of the actions and reusable workflows you reference.
This repository's own workflows (the deploy and daily-check ones) are the kind of file it validates.

sections.title: Get started
items: Sign in with your GitHub account and allow GitHub Actions access when prompted. Open a GitHub repository. The syntax features work in workflow files, and a GitHub Actions icon appears in the Activity Bar.

entries.name: GitLens — Git supercharged
entries.summary: Git blame, history and graph tools inside VS Code. Off by default: the basics are free, but part of it is a paid plan and the README promotes a Pro trial.
entries.license: MIT, except the `plus` folder, which has its own licence

version.name: GitLens — Git supercharged extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.101.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: GitLens Community is "free and open-source, forever": blame, hovers, CodeLens, file annotations, revision navigation, the side bar views, the Interactive Rebase Editor, the Git Command Palette and integrations. On public repositories the Commit Graph, Worktrees and Visual History are free too, and the Commit Graph needs a free GitKraken account.

Pro opens those on private repositories and adds more: the Pull Requests panel with in-graph review and merge, Launchpad, agent sessions and the AI features. The README offers a 14-day Pro trial. Features marked Preview need a free GitKraken account and may become Pro features.
The licence is MIT for everything outside a folder named `plus`, which is covered by a separate licence file.

sections.title: Why it is off
items: A judgement, not a finding: VS Code's built-in Git support and the GitHub Pull Requests extension cover most daily use. Turn GitLens on in `profile.json` if you want blame annotations and the graph. The graph on private repositories is a Pro feature.

sections.title: Reference

entries.name: ShellCheck
entries.summary: ShellCheck for shell scripts, as you type, with quick fixes. It bundles ShellCheck, so no binary needs installing.

version.name: ShellCheck extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.101.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: It reports ShellCheck's warnings in the editor and the Problems view, as you type or on save, and offers quick fixes and Fix All for a file. It bundles precompiled ShellCheck binaries for Linux (x86_64, arm64 and arm), so it works in WSL without `apt install shellcheck`. It reads your `.shellcheckrc`.
This repository's `setup.sh` scripts are what it checks.

sections.title: Use it
items: Open a shell script. Hover a problem for its rule code and a link to the rule. The ShellCheck icon in the status bar opens a menu to lint now or change when it runs. Commands: `ShellCheck: Lint Current Document`, `ShellCheck: Show Menu`.

items.title: Install from a terminal

items: To apply every automatic fix on save the README uses `"editor.codeActionsOnSave": {"source.fixAll.shellcheck": "explicit"}`. `setup.sh` does not set it: it would change scripts without asking.

entries.summary: TOML support backed by Taplo: highlighting, validation, formatting and JSON-schema completion. Off by default: the latest release is from December 2024 and its README calls it a preview extension.

version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.90.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Useful for `pyproject.toml` (uv) and `starship.toml`: TOML 1.0.0 support, semantic highlighting, validation, folding, a symbol tree, renaming, formatting, and completion and validation with JSON Schema.
The README says it is "currently a preview extension, it might contain bugs, or might even crash". The last Marketplace release is 0.21.2 from 2024-12-20. That is why it is off.

sections.title: Turn it on
items: Set it to `true` in `profile.json` and run `setup.sh --only toml`. No settings are merged for it.

entries.name: EditorConfig
entries.summary: Applies a project's `.editorconfig` over your VS Code settings. Off by default: it only matters in repositories that have the file.

version.name: EditorConfig extension
version.docs: Marketplace stable build (not the pre-release). README read 2026-10-29. Needs VS Code 1.100.0 or newer.

sections.title: In one minute
items: The extension "attempts to override user/workspace settings with settings found in .editorconfig files". Supported properties: `indent_style`, `indent_size`, `tab_width`, `end_of_line`, `insert_final_newline` and `trim_trailing_whitespace` (the last three on save), and `charset`.
Without `root=true` in the file, EditorConfig keeps looking in parent folders.

sections.title: How it meets the profile
items: The profile sets `files.eol`, `files.insertFinalNewline` and `files.trimTrailingWhitespace` for every folder. With this extension on, a project's `.editorconfig` wins for the same properties.

entries.name: Settings that setup.sh writes
entries.summary: What the profile merges into your user settings.json, where VS Code keeps settings, and what the script will and will not touch.

version.name: VS Code settings
version.docs: code.visualstudio.com/docs/configure/settings (dated 2026-10-28) and each extension's README

notes: The exact Windows family name of the Nerd Font was not confirmed. The setting lists four spellings and VS Code uses the first that is installed; the Nerd Fonts FAQ says to use a font with 'Nerd Font Mono' (NFM) in the name for monospaced icons, and VS Code's docs show a Nerd Font as 'Hack NF'.
The path of the Remote (WSL) settings file was not in the pages read, so the script writes only to the user settings file. The user settings apply in WSL windows too.
`files.trimTrailingWhitespace` is off for Markdown because two trailing spaces end a line there; that rule is Markdown's, not from the VS Code pages read.
Whether `terraform fmt` output differs between Terraform versions was not checked. ESLint was not compared with a CI command here; its README was not read for how it picks the project's ESLint.

sections.title: In one minute
items: `setup.sh` merges groups of settings from the `settings` part of [profile.json](../setup/profile.json) into the Windows user `settings.json`. A group is skipped when the extension it needs is not on, so a formatter is never set for an extension you do not have.

sections.title: Where settings live
items: Later scopes override earlier ones: default, user, remote, workspace, workspace folder, then the language-specific version of each, and finally policy settings set by an administrator. The script writes to user settings, so a project's `.vscode/settings.json` or `.editorconfig` can still override it.

rows: Every VS Code window, including WSL windows.
Windows opened on that WSL distribution.
That project, for everyone who opens it.
items.caption: From the VS Code settings and WSL docs.

items: Language-specific blocks such as `"[python]": {...}` override non-language settings, even from a narrower scope.

sections.title: What each group does
items: `files`: `files.eol` set to `\n` so files keep LF (the WSL docs advise consistent line endings between Windows and Linux); a final newline and no trailing whitespace on save, except in Markdown. All three setting names are in VS Code's source.
`python_ruff`, `eslint`, `prettier`, `terraform`: the formatters and save actions from the extensions' READMEs. They are described in the Python, JavaScript and Terraform tabs.
`terminal_font`: sets `terminal.integrated.fontFamily` to a Nerd Font so the Starship prompt shows its icons in VS Code's terminal. The font must be installed on Windows first.

items.title: A Nerd Font in the terminal (VS Code's own example)

items: `hide_copilot`: off by default. VS Code has AI features built in, and signing in to Copilot enrols an eligible account in Copilot Free. `chat.disableAIFeatures` "disables and hides features like chat or inline suggestions in VS Code and disables the Copilot extension". Run `setup.sh --only hide_copilot` to apply it.

sections.title: Format like CI does
items: Format Document is `Shift+Alt+F` on Windows (`Ctrl+K Ctrl+F` formats the selection). It is VS Code's default, so setup.sh does not set it. It and format on save call the same formatter, so what they produce is what the extension's tool produces.
To match CI, the formatter must be the tool the pipeline runs, with the same version and the same config file. The profile already picks the same tool; the rest depends on the project:

rows: `terraform` on the PATH inside Ubuntu. If it is not found, formatting silently fails.
The Ruff version. The extension ships its own, but prefers the one in the project's Python environment, then the PATH. Pin the CI version in the project.
The extension uses the project's own `prettier` in `node_modules` when there is one, and reads the project's config file. With `prettier.requireConfig` on, a project without one is not formatted.
items.caption: Commands from the Terraform, Ruff and Prettier CLI docs; extension behaviour from their READMEs.

items.title: tflint is not a formatter
items.text: TFLint is a linter, run from the command line or in the pipeline. Its README mentions no VS Code extension, and it describes no formatter (its `--fix` fixes lint issues). Run `tflint` in the Ubuntu terminal for the same result as CI; format on save is `terraform fmt`.

items.title: Ruff format does not sort imports
items.text: The Ruff docs say the formatter does not sort imports; that is done by `ruff check --select I --fix`. The profile sorts imports on save through a separate code action. If CI only runs `ruff format --check`, imports are not what it checks.

items: To see which Ruff is in use, run `Ruff: Print debug information` or `Ruff: Show server logs`. Terraform's `terraform fmt` has no config file. For Prettier and Ruff, the project's own `.prettierrc` or `ruff.toml` decides, which is also what CI reads.

sections.title: Install the font
items: From WSL bash: `winget.exe install DEVCOM.JetBrainsMonoNerdFont` (winget.exe is on the WSL PATH; PowerShell is not needed) (the package exists in the winget-pkgs repository). Then restart VS Code. Windows Terminal needs the same font set in its Ubuntu profile.

sections.title: What the script will not do
items: It makes a timestamped backup next to the file before changing it.
A settings file with comments is not rewritten: JSON has no comments, so rewriting would drop them. The script prints what it would change and stops. A file that is not valid JSON is also left alone.
A value you set yourself that differs from the profile is replaced by the profile's value. The dry run prints it as `change` first, with the old value.
Run `setup.sh --dry-run` to see every change before it is made.
